title: The reproductive success of a threatened bird in regenerating forest: Habitat structure and the limited legacy of tree planting
content:
These results highlight the link between habitat characteristics in regenerating forest and successful breeding of threatened species. In practice, these findings could directly inform species management by prioritising areas with more favourable habitat for supportive breeding interventions, such as nest box placement. Our results also suggest that, while the planting of some tree species (e.g. Leptospermum scoparium) may promote tree species richness in regenerating forest, diverse or species-rich tree plantings do not necessarily translate to improved forest regeneration. This has broader implications for other reforestation projects in similar landscapes, suggesting that restoration efforts need not be constrained by limited access to a wide diversity of native tree species.


Abstract

Forest restoration is a key conservation strategy, often with the goal of providing suitable habitat for threatened animal species. The success of forest restoration therefore lies in the long-term improved fitness of threatened species; however, forest restoration success is rarely measured in this way. We use a combination of data collected from (a) a large-scale, historical community planting project on Tiritiri Matangi Island sanctuary in Aotearoa New Zealand, (b) contemporary habitat surveys of the island and (c) long-term breeding records of a reintroduced threatened forest-specialist bird species, the hihi (Notiomystis cincta). With this data, we examine how past tree-planting practices have influenced habitat structure in a regenerating forest, and how these habitat characteristics affect the reproductive success of a species of conservation concern. Our results show that habitat structure is strongly associated with hihi breeding success. Hihi nesting in forest areas with a taller and denser upper canopy has higher egg hatching success and fledges greater numbers of chicks. Although the tree-planting project initiated restoration of the forest, our results show that the specific planting regimen applied across the island had a limited impact on the contemporary composition and structure of the forest. In fact, tree communities in the regenerating forest have diverged rapidly from the species that were planted. Synthesis and Applications. These results highlight the link between habitat characteristics in regenerating forest and successful breeding of threatened species. In practice, these findings could directly inform species management by prioritising areas with more favourable habitat for supportive breeding interventions, such as nest box placement. Our results also suggest that, while the planting of some tree species (e.g. Leptospermum scoparium) may promote tree species richness in regenerating forest, diverse or species-rich tree plantings do not necessarily translate to improved forest regeneration. This has broader implications for other reforestation projects in similar landscapes, suggesting that restoration efforts need not be constrained by limited access to a wide diversity of native tree species.
